name: Estrogen topical for hair

lead: Topical estrogen for hair usually means alfatradiol (17-alpha-estradiol), a weak estrogen scalp solution sold in Germany and parts of Latin America for pattern hair loss. People use it to slow thinning and keep what they have.

It binds estrogen receptors weakly and inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, reducing conversion of testosterone to DHT and so follicle shrinkage. Studies report it slowing or stabilizing loss without increasing density or thickness, and minoxidil outperformed it in a 103-woman study.

paras: It is an alcohol-based solution applied to the scalp as a long-term routine, sometimes alongside other thinning-hair treatments.
Scalp irritation from the alcohol vehicle and more oil production are reported. Labeling advises against use in pregnancy and under age 18.

angle.text: Scalp estrogen solutions, mainly alfatradiol, weakly block 5-alpha-reductase so less DHT reaches the follicle, which slows shrinkage and thinning. Studies describe slowed or stabilized loss rather than added density.

lead: Topical estrogen for hair refers to estrogenic solutions applied to the scalp for pattern hair loss. The best-documented example is alfatradiol (17-alpha-estradiol), a weak estrogen and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor sold as an ethanol-based scalp solution in Germany and some Latin American countries under names such as Ell-Cranell Alpha [1].

Wikipedia reports that alfatradiol slowed or stabilized hair loss in studies without increasing hair density or thickness, and that minoxidil outperformed it in a 103-woman study [1]. More generally, estrogen is associated with thicker hair during pregnancy, and estradiol has documented skin effects, but its role as a hair-loss treatment is not established in the general sources reviewed [2][3].
infobox: Germany, parts of Latin America; Rx-only in the US [1]

paras: Alfatradiol is a stereoisomer of 17-beta-estradiol, binds estrogen receptors with much lower estrogenic activity, and inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, which converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone [1].

Local burning or itching, attributed to the ethanol vehicle, and increased sebum production are reported for alfatradiol; its leaflet advises against use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under age 18 [1]. Estradiol more broadly is associated with clotting and hormone-sensitive cancer risks in general discussions, though these are described for estrogen use overall rather than topical scalp products specifically [3].

A 1980 controlled trial of alfatradiol in androgenetic alopecia reported reduced hair loss without new growth, and a later university-led study in 103 women found minoxidil more effective than alfatradiol [1]. No studies were found in the sources reviewed for topical 17-beta-estradiol or other estrogen preparations specifically for hair loss.

timeline.event: A controlled trial of alfatradiol in androgenetic alopecia is reported [1].
